messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I have what I think is a list of data frames and I want to break the list into its data frames. I am importing a series of files into R using these two lines of code

yieldfiles <- paste0("/accessdata/yield", c("corn.csv", "cc.csv","tomato.csv","wheat.csv"))
yield <- lapply(yieldfiles, read.csv, header=TRUE, sep = ",", stringsAsFactors=FALSE)

When I do this, I get a list of data frames. I use the command

yield[[1]]

or

yield[1]

to access the first data frame in the list.

What I want to do is split this list up into its component data frames. I think I should use split(), but I'm not sure what the f argument would be. Of course if there is a better way to import the data so I don't have to do this that would also be cool. Thanks!

Elise

One quick thought —

You may not want to load each dataframe into your environment. This may be so-called "code smell". If your dataframes have the same columns, it might be better to attach a column indicating the sample name, and then use a do.call/rbind to rbind each dataframe together. This way, your data comes together more easily and this can make downstream analysis much easier.

But this all depends on what you're doing downstream — using list2env may be entirely appropriate for what you're doing.

Hope this helps,
Vince

messages.subject: ANOVA with nested random and fixed effects: help!
messages.subject_clean: ANOVA with nested random and fixed effects: help!
messages.body_plain:
Hello R friends,

I am stuck on an analysis I'm doing for my advisor's experiment that involves an anova with multiple layers of nesting of random and fixed effects. In this experiment, there are three sites, with five blocks per site. Each block is divided into two watering treatments (plots), and in each plot there are two priority planting treatments (sub-plots). So, it's kind of a split-split plot design, but I was advised to analyze this as a repeated measures experiment, with blocks counting as the repeated measures. Block is the only random factor, and site, water, and planting treatment are fixed effects.

We want to test the effects of planting treatment, watering treatment, site, and all 2- and 3-way interactions on native and invasive plant cover using anova. The thing that seems to be tripping me up the most is the fact that there's a random effect (Block) sandwiched between fixed effects, (the nesting structure goes: Site/Block/Water/Planting Treatment), and I don't know how to code this properly.

I suspect that we may not have enough degrees of freedom to analyze this correctly. Another option is to ignore the nesting of block within site, which would make blocks simple replicates of the water*planting treatment combinations.(Technically this is pseudoreplication, but it could also be thought of as a stratified random sample of sites.)

I have been trying to use lme from the nlme package. (Apparently lme4 does not give p-values, and we want those.) My consultations with a statistician and myriad online and print resources have resulted in a number of attempts, but I am not convinced any of them are correct. Maybe you can help!

Here are some attempts so far:

#This one ignores nesting of block within site, but includes the other levels of nesting
mod1=lme(Cover~ Site*Water*PlantingTrt,
          random=~1|Block/Water/PlantingTrt)

#This one includes the full nesting structure, but I'm not sure everything should go in the random statement. Plus I get NaNs for Site.
mod2=lme(Cover~ Site*Water*PlantingTrt,
          random=~1|Site/Block/Water/PlantingTrt)

#This one uses the aov function instead, and I got this code from this <http://www.personal.psu.edu/mar36/stat_461/split_plot/split_plot.html> example. The results are very different from anything above.
mod3 = aov(Cover ~ Site * Water * PlantingTrt + Error(Block/Site:Water))

I would greatly appreciate any advice on this!

Thanks,
Emily

Emily Peffer
PhD candidate
Graduate Group in Ecology
Department of Plant Sciences
University of California, Davis
Office: (530) 752-2667

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Mark Lubell suggested some of us might be interested in this new (free) book on statistical learning: http://www-bcf.usc.edu/~gareth/ISL/index.html. It looks pretty accessible and is taught through examples in R. Cheers,

Michael

>From the preface:

Statistical learning refers to a set of tools for modeling and understanding
complex datasets. It is a recently developed area in statistics and blends
with parallel developments in computer science and, in particular, machine
learning. The field encompasses many methods such as the lasso and sparse
regression, classification and regression trees, and boosting and support
vector machines.
With the explosion of “Big Data” problems, statistical learning has become
a very hot field in many scientific areas as well as marketing, finance,
and other business disciplines. People with statistical learning skills are in
high demand.
One of the first books in this area—The Elements of Statistical Learning
(ESL) (Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman)—was published in 2001, with a
second edition in 2009. ESL has become a popular text not only in statistics
but also in related fields. One of the reasons for ESL’s popularity is
its relatively accessible style. But ESL is intended for individuals with advanced
training in the mathematical sciences. An Introduction to Statistical
Learning (ISL) arose from the perceived need for a broader and less technical
treatment of these topics. In this new book, we cover many of the
same topics as ESL, but we concentrate more on the applications of the
methods and less on the mathematical details. We have created labs illustrating
how to implement each of the statistical learning methods using the
popular statistical software package R. These labs provide the reader with
valuable hands-on experience.

messages.body_plain:
OK, I have a quick, perhaps point missing question:
Are the watering and planting treatments really different per block?

It seems surprising if they are, but if they're not, and if you were specifying RE on them, I think you would be in the territory of crossed effects (i.e. the the watering or planting treatments not being properly nested within site, or at least within block). BUT, it sounds to me like you don't want any RE on either water or planting.

Now, my take:

>From your description you don't want RE on Site either, so in that case my interpretation of the question is how to specify RE on block alone, which is:

mod4  = lme(Cover ~ Site*Water*PlantingTrt, random=~1|Block)

This corresponds to a model where observation i in block j of site k

Cover_i,j,k ~ Intercept + Site_k*Water_i*Planting_i + Intercept_j

where Intercept_j ~ Normal(0, sigma_block) # where sigma_block estimated across all blocks.
I believe the lme code above for mod4 would do this so long as every block has a unique number.

Also see the recent paper in methods in ecology and evolution relevant to this issue:
- Schielzeth, Nakagawa_2013_Nested by design model fitting and interpretation in a mixed model era

- Jaime

Thanks for the comments thus far!

Jaime- To answer what I think is your question, there aren't major differences in treatment effects across different blocks, but there are some, particularly for one site. One thing mod4 doesn't do is specify the fact that planting treatment is nested in the watering treatment. Because block is first split into watering treatment, and then planting treatments are randomized within watering treatment, this becomes a split-plot design. I think I need to specify random~1|Block/Water/PlantingTrt to do this, otherwise we run into pseudoreplication issues (which may or may not be that egregious depending on your perspective).

messages.subject: Bootstrapping
messages.subject_clean: Bootstrapping
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I have series of functions that are used to predict 3 different growth stages and optimize (best fit 1:1 line between predicted and observed) the Base, Lower, and Upper temperature thresholds (used in calculating degree days) for 9 varieties (see below). What I Like to do is to see if the distribution of these temperatures are significantly different from each other. In other word, I like to use same temperature for all varieties. I talked to Emilio Laca and he suggested that I do bootstrapping (boot and boot.ci <http://boot.ci> function) on my data. My problem is that I can't connect the functions with bootstrap. Any idea?

e <- read.csv("TempField_All.csv", stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
h <- read.csv("FieldStages.csv", stringsAsFactors=FALSE)

library(boot)
library(parallel)

# Make dates uniform
e$date <- as.Date(e$date, "%m/%d/%y")
h$Planting <- as.Date(h$Planting, "%m/%d/%y")
h$PI <- as.Date(h$PI, "%m/%d/%y")
h$Heading <- as.Date(h$Heading, "%m/%d/%y")
h$R7 <- as.Date(h$R7, "%m/%d/%y")

# Bootstrapping
my.cor <- function(data, i) {
  bootsample <- data[i,]

#Prepare and calculate Degree Days

prepareEnv <- function(v, e, basetemp, LowerT, UpperT) {
  ev <- e[e$ID==v$ID, ]
  ev$Tx[ev$Tx > UpperT] <- UpperT
  ev$Tn[ev$Tn < LowerT] <- LowerT
  ev$tmean <- (ev$Tn + ev$Tx) / 2
  end <- v$R7
  if (is.na <http://is.na>(end)) end <- v$Planting + 150
  ev <- ev[which(ev$date == v$Planting) : which(ev$date==end), ]
  ev$csum <- cumsum(ev$tmean - basetemp)
  ev
}

linearTT <- function(env, obs, tmp, ...) {
  basetemp <- tmp[1]
  LowerT <- tmp[2]
  UpperT <- tmp[3]
  if (LowerT > UpperT | basetemp < 0 | UpperT > 50) {
    return(rep(Inf,3))
  }
  ev <- prepareEnv(obs, env, basetemp, LowerT, UpperT)

  tt_pi <- sum(ev$tmean[ev$date <= obs$PI] - basetemp)
  tt_hd <- sum(ev$tmean[ev$date <= obs$Heading] - basetemp)
  tt_mt <- sum(ev$tmean[ev$date <= obs$R7] - basetemp)
  c(tt_pi, tt_hd, tt_mt)
}

predictLinearTT <- function(env, obs, tmp, pars, ...) {
  basetemp <- tmp[1]
  LowerT <- tmp[2]
  UpperT <- tmp[3]
  ev <- prepareEnv(obs, env, basetemp, LowerT, UpperT)
  pi <-  max(which(ev$csum < pars[1]))
  hd <- max(which(ev$csum < pars[2]))
  mt <- max(which(ev$csum < pars[3]))
  data.frame(pi, hd, mt)
}

fun <- function(parms, returnData=FALSE) {

  res <- matrix(nrow=nrow(v), ncol=3, dimnames=list(list(), list('pi', 'hd', 'mt')))
  for (i in 1:nrow(v)) {
    res[i,1:3] <- fitmodel(e, v[i,,drop=FALSE], parms)
  }
  m <- colMeans(res, na.rm=TRUE)

  rd <- matrix(nrow=nrow(v), ncol=6, dimnames=list(list(), list('o_pi', 'p_pi', 'o_hd', 'p_hd', 'o_mt', 'p_mt')))
  for (i in 1:nrow(v)) {
    o_pi <- as.integer(v$PI[i] - v$Planting[i])
    o_hd <- as.integer(v$Heading[i] - v$Planting[i])
    o_mt <- as.integer(v$R7[i] - v$Planting[i])

    p <- predictmodel(e, v[i,,drop=FALSE], parms, m)
    rd[i, ] <- c(o_pi, p$pi, o_hd, p$hd, o_mt, p$mt)
  }

  if (returnData) {
    return(rd)
  } else {
    tpi <- na.omit(rd[, 1:2])
    return( sum(abs(tpi[,2] - tpi[,1])) )
  }
}

fitmodel = linearTT
predictmodel = predictLinearTT

vars <- unique(h$Varieties)

v <- h[h$Varieties==vars[1], ]
op= optim(c(12, 12, 33), fun)

res2 <- res <- list()
for (i in 1:length(vars)) {
  v <- h[h$Varieties==vars[i], ]
  res[[i]] <- optim(c(12, 12, 33), fun)
  res2[[i]] <- fun(res[[i]]$par, returnData=TRUE)
}
  return(data.frame(vars, t(sapply(res, function(x)x$par))))
}

boot.cor <- boot(data= h, statistic = my.cor, R= 1000, strata= h$Varieties)
plot(boot.cor)
boot.ci <http://boot.ci>(boot.cor, index=1, type="bcd")

Thanks,
Hussain

But one other thing I notice is if site and plantingTrt are categorical data, then the output of you result should have some dummy variables but not what is shown in your result, so maybe you should change the numeric to factor?
Last, I think using 'marginal' might be more appropriate, it seems like sequential is used if you assume the effect is additive (i.e no interaction) which is not the assumption in your case. But I am not 100% sure.
Currently I am taking the class that teaches us mixed model, so I should consult with professor to more adivise.

On Monday, January 13, 2014 5:46:57 PM UTC-8, Emily Peffer wrote:

> Hello R friends,
>
> I am stuck on an analysis I'm doing for my advisor's experiment that involves an anova with multiple layers of nesting of random and fixed effects. In this experiment, there are three sites, with five blocks per site. Each block is divided into two watering treatments (plots), and in each plot there are two priority planting treatments (sub-plots). So, it's kind of a split-split plot design, but I was advised to analyze this as a repeated measures experiment, with blocks counting as the repeated measures. Block is the only random factor, and site, water, and planting treatment are fixed effects.
>
> We want to test the effects of planting treatment, watering treatment, site, and all 2- and 3-way interactions on native and invasive plant cover using anova. The thing that seems to be tripping me up the most is the fact that there's a random effect (Block) sandwiched between fixed effects, (the nesting structure goes: Site/Block/Water/Planting Treatment), and I don't know how to code this properly.
>
> I suspect that we may not have enough degrees of freedom to analyze this correctly. Another option is to ignore the nesting of block within site, which would make blocks simple replicates of the water*planting treatment combinations.(Technically this is pseudoreplication, but it could also be thought of as a stratified random sample of sites.)
>
> I have been trying to use lme from the nlme package. (Apparently lme4 does not give p-values, and we want those.) My consultations with a statistician and myriad online and print resources have resulted in a number of attempts, but I am not convinced any of them are correct. Maybe you can help!
>
> Here are some attempts so far:
>
> #This one ignores nesting of block within site, but includes the other levels of nesting
> mod1=lme(Cover~ Site*Water*PlantingTrt,
>           random=~1|Block/Water/PlantingTrt)
>
> #This one includes the full nesting structure, but I'm not sure everything should go in the random statement. Plus I get NaNs for Site.
> mod2=lme(Cover~ Site*Water*PlantingTrt,
>           random=~1|Site/Block/Water/PlantingTrt)
>
> #This one uses the aov function instead, and I got this code from this <http://www.personal.psu.edu/mar36/stat_461/split_plot/split_plot.html> example. The results are very different from anything above.
> mod3 = aov(Cover ~ Site * Water * PlantingTrt + Error(Block/Site:Water))
>
>
> I would greatly appreciate any advice on this!
>
> Thanks,
> Emily

messages.body_plain:
Yu Pei (and others),

I got some more advice on how to do this, and what was recommended to me was assigning a new variable with a unique main plot ID (as a reminder, watering treatments are assigned to main plots within blocks, and planting treatments to subplots within main plots), and then specifying the random statement like this:

random=~1|Block/MainPlot

Turns out, this gives me the same results as specifying the error term like this (as I had done before):

random=~1|Block/Water/PlantingTrt

This might be because I only have one replication of water*planting treatment per block, but it is a good sign! (I suspect the first way might be the best way to do it if I had replications within blocks, but I haven't actually thought this through. I should also note that I assigned unique IDs to blocks, and told R they were factors. All the effects are factors.)

I was also told that Type I (sequential) SS were best for this design, so that is also good.

I think I'm all set on this now, but it's been fun geeking out with you all!

Thanks,
Emily

messages.body_plain:
Hi Greg,

In the file you attached, your SAR function uses Strikes and strikes inconsistently. R is case-sensitive so it’s looking for two variables:
SAR = function(Strikes, M, a) {
    Strikes*M/(a + strikes)
}

When I run the file I get this different error:
Error in SAR(x, M = 0.8, a = 3) : object 'strikes' not found

When I changed the last strikes in the function to Strikes, everything worked fine. I suspect that you had a value for strikes somewhere in your environment which obscured this error.

Vince will not forgive me if I don’t also point out that using attach is often problematic because for just this reason - you end up with variables in your environment that are difficult to track. Better to refer to the data frame directly (data$Rep) or wrap your code in a with() function.

Noam
